question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable at a Point
question.problem: At an ice cream shop, on average, $25%$ of customers buy chocolate ice cream. What is the probability that the $4$th customer of the day is the first person buying a chocolate ice cream? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of customers that enter the ice cream shop until the first one buys a chocolate ice cream. Since the chance of a customer buying a chocolate ice cream is $25%,$ the number of customers before the first buys a chocolate ice cream can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=25%=\frac{25}{100}=0.25.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.25).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.25)^{x-1}(0.25) \\  & =(0.75)^{x-1}(0.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the $4$th customer of the day is the first buying a chocolate ice cream is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =(0.75)^{4-1}(0.25) \\  & =(0.75)^{3}(0.25) \\  & ≈0.105\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable on a Bounded Interval
question.problem: A card is being randomly picked from a standard $52$ cards deck and put back in until getting a red card. What is the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of cards picked until a red one is chosen. Since there are $26$ red cards in a $52$ cards deck, the chance of choosing a red card is $\frac{26}{52}.$ Thus, the number of chosen cards before getting a red card can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=\frac{26}{52}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.5).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.5)^{x-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)^{x-1}(0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 5) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3,4,5\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & =(0.5)^{1-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{2-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{5-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)+(0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)^{2}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4}(0.5) \\  & =[1+0.5+(0.5)^{2}+(0.5)^{3}+(0.5)^{4}](0.5) \\  & ≈0.969\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

judgment.reasoning: Replacement makes the draws independent, each with red-card probability 1/2. The probability of at least one red card in five draws is 1−(1/2)^5=31/32=0.96875, which rounds to 0.969. This agrees with the captured worked solution.
